dataset.name: Soil moisture, physical and chemical properties coincident with airborne SAR data collections for 2017 and 2019, Seward Peninsula, Alaska
description: Soil samples were collected coincident with in-situ soil moisture and thaw depth measurements at NGEE Arctic study sites on the Seward Peninsula, Alaska in August 2017 and 2019 Field measurements and flights were conducted during both summers as a collaboration between the NASA ABoVE Project's Airborne SAR Campaign and the NGEE Arctic Project. Airborne overflights of L-band SAR instruments occurred during the soil sampling periods. Laboratory measurements of soil properties include bulk density, volumetric and gravimetric water content, carbon and nitrogen content, and particle size of mineral components. Soil samples processed and reported in this dataset were collected coincident with in situ measurements of soil moisture and thaw depth and airborne P-band and L-band SAR measurements as a collaboration between NGEE Arctic and NASA ABoVE. To learn more about how ABoVE protocols were applied for sampling site selection and making in situ measurements, see the following datasets: (2017: https://doi.org/10.5440/1423892 and 2019: https://doi.org/10.5440/1856042). Contained in this dataset are four .csv data files (including data dictionaries) and one zipped folder of *.pdf files.

The Next-Generation Ecosystem Experiments: Arctic (NGEE Arctic), was a research effort (with some overlap with Covid-19 pandemic) to reduce uncertainty in Earth System Models by developing a predictive understanding of carbon-rich Arctic ecosystems and feedbacks to climate. NGEE Arctic was supported by the Department of Energy's Office of Biological and Environmental Research.

The NGEE Arctic project had two field research sites: 1) located within the Arctic polygonal tundra coastal region on the Barrow Environmental Observatory (BEO) and the North Slope near Utqiagvik (Barrow), Alaska and 2) multiple areas on the discontinuous permafrost region of the Seward Peninsula north of Nome, Alaska.

Through observations, experiments, and synthesis with existing datasets, NGEE Arctic provided an enhanced knowledge base for multi-scale modeling and contributed to improved process representation at global pan-Arctic scales within the Department of Energy's Earth system Model (the Energy Exascale Earth System Model, or E3SM), and specifically within the E3SM Land Model component (ELM).

measurementTechnique:
For consistency with the SAR study, the ABoVE protocols for sampling and measuring soil moisture and thaw depth were followed. ABoVE protocols are included as companion files.
Field sample collection:
Because this dataset was collected to aid in ground-truthing remotely-sensed moisture data, our sampling protocols differ from traditional soil sampling methods. The SAR instrument does not distinguish between the ground surface (including vegetation) and the soil surface, thus, this soil sample dataset includes surface vegetation in its reported measurements. To aid users of this dataset, samples were classified as vegetation, organic soil, or mineral soil.
Samples were collected at select SAR flags (see companion files and in situ datasets; 2017: https://doi.org/10.5440/1423892 and 2019: link to https://doi.org/10.5440/1856042). Flags where we collected soil samples sampled in 2017 were not resampled in 2019.
In 2017, rectangular blocks of soil were cut from each flag location using a bread knife. At each flag, samples were vertically split based on horizonation, determined visually as a shift in a vegetative, duff, or mineral layer. Samples were weighed, stored in plastic bags and refrigerated. Samples that were large enough were subsampled with a tin of known volume in the lab to measure dry bulk density and volumetric water content.
In 2019, samples were collected in containers of known volume. To match ABoVE SAR ground-truthing protocols, samples were collected at depth increments that matched in situ soil moisture probe depths (0-6 cm, 6-12 cm, 12-20 cm).

Dry bulk density:
For soil collected in 2017, subsamples were collected with tins of known volume. Samples were dried in an oven at 105°C for 24 hours. Bulk density was not calculated if the soil contained too much plant material (common for samples from the upper soil profile) or it was impossible to subsample a known volume from the larger samples.
For soil collected in 2019, samples were dried in their sample containers at 105°C for 24 hours.
Bulk density was calculated using the following equation:
Db = (g oven dry soil)/(〖cm〗^3 (sampling container volume))

Gravimetric water content:
Samples from both years were weighed in the field after collection and after oven drying at 105°C for 24 hours to measure the soil water content. Gravimetric water content was calculated using the following equation:
GWC = (g water [field weight(g)-dry weight (g)])/(g dry soil (weight of both dry samples))
Volumetric Water Content (lab):
Volumetric water content was calculated using the following equation:
VWC = Db X GWC X 100% = (〖cm〗^3 water)/(〖cm〗^3 soil) X 100%
Volumetric water content was not calculated if bulk density was not calculated.
Volumetric Water Content (in situ, measured horizontally with Hydrosense II)
Volumetric water content data were collected using a Hydrosense II soil-water sensor and data logger which collected the GPS location of the moisture samples. Hydrosense sensor rely on soil dielectric properties to estimate volumetric water content (VWC).
After a sample was collected from the pit, the Hydrosense II probe was inserted horizontally into the soil profile at the middle depth of the sample depth range. The moisture value and probe period were recorded on data sheets in the field following ABoVE protocol (See https://doi.org/10.5440/1423892 (2017 dataset) and https://doi.org/10.5440/1856042 (2019 dataset).

Particle size by pipette method
Particle size analysis was performed by the Desert Research Institute in Reno, Nevada. Dry samples were shipped to the Soil Characterization and Quaternary Pedology Lab for processing. At the DRI, samples were sieved with a 2 mm gravel sieve. The <2mm samples were split using a Gilson micro splitter for loss on ignition and texture analysis.
Organic matter from highly organic samples was removed with the addition of 3 to 5 mL of a 30% hydrogen peroxide solution. On a hot plate at 70°C an additional 3 to 5 mL of hydrogen peroxide solution was added every 10 minutes until foaming subsided.
The <2 mm fraction of samples underwent sample dispersion using a 10% sodium pyrophosphate solution on a shaker for 6 hours. The samples were wet sieved with DI water and a 63 µm sieve. Sample fractions < 63 µm were retained in a fleaker for pipette texture analysis. The fraction of sample >63 µm was retained for dry sieving.
The fleaker containing the fraction of the sample <63 µm was filled to 1200 mL and shaken for 45 seconds to disperse the sample. Two 25 mL aliquots are taken from the fleaker at 10 cm depth and placed into a pre-weighed aluminum weighing dish. One aliquot is collected immediately after shaking and the second is collected later based on fleaker temperature to determine the 2 µm settling time to 10 cm (approximately 7.5 hours). The two aliquots are weighed to determine silt and clay content.
The >63 µm fraction of each sample (sand) was dry sieved using 3 in sieves and placed on a Gilson sieve shaker for 10 minutes.

Carbon and nitrogen content via elemental analyzer
%C and %N were measured on most samples at the Geology and Geochemical Research Laboratory at Los Alamos National Laboratory in Los Alamos, New Mexico. Samples were crushed with mortar and pestle for homogenization. Approximately 5 mg of sample was weighed and folded into aluminum tins for analysis in a Eurovector elemental analyzer coupled to an Isoprime isotope ratio mass spectrometer.
Organic carbon content via environmental analyzer
Organic carbon content was measured using a Eurovector elemental analyzer coupled to an Isoprime isotope ratio mass spectrometer. Approximately 5 mg of sample was weighed into silver tin capsules and treated with 6N hydrochloric acid at 50°C to remove inorganic carbon prior to analysis.
